questions.question: Over about four weeks, the Moon goes from a thin crescent to a round, bright full moon, and then back to a crescent again. What makes the Moon's shape seem to change?
questions.answer: A bigger or smaller part of its sunlit half faces Earth
choices: A bigger or smaller part of its sunlit half faces Earth
Earth's shadow covers a bigger or smaller part of it
The Sun lights a bigger or smaller part of it
Other planets' shadows cover a bigger or smaller part of it
questions.context: The Sun always lights one half of the Moon. As the Moon travels round Earth, a bigger or smaller part of that sunlit half is turned toward Earth. Earth's shadow plays no part in the phases: it falls on the Moon only in a lunar eclipse.
questions.grade_note: Why the Moon has phases, and that Earth's shadow is not the cause, is the heart of the 6th-grade Sun-Earth-Moon unit (NGSS MS-ESS1-1).

questions.question: At new moon, the side of the Moon that faces Earth is dark, and the Moon cannot be seen in the sky at all. What is the far side of the Moon like at that moment?
questions.answer: Lit all over by the Sun
choices: Lit all over by the Sun
Dark, as it always is
Dark, in Earth's shadow
Half lit and half dark
questions.context: The Sun always lights half of the Moon, and at new moon that sunlit half is the far side, turned away from Earth. The far side is often called the dark side, but it gets just as much sunlight as the side people see from Earth.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade phase lessons teach that one half of the Moon is always lit, and the far side's sunlit new moon corrects the dark-side myth.

questions.question: A full moon shines on a clear night. Over the next two weeks, its lit part changes night by night until the Moon is new again. Which phases does it pass through, in order?
questions.answer: Waning gibbous, third quarter, waning crescent
choices: Waning gibbous, third quarter, waning crescent
Waxing gibbous, first quarter, waxing crescent
Waning crescent, third quarter, waning gibbous
Waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous
questions.context: After full moon the lit part shrinks, and a shrinking Moon is waning. It is gibbous first, more than half lit, then a half circle at third quarter, then a thin crescent before new moon. Waxing means growing: the waxing phases come in the two weeks before full moon.
questions.grade_note: The eight phases in order, with waxing and waning, are the standard 6th-grade phase sequence.

questions.question: A full moon comes up just as the Sun goes down. It shines all night and sets as the Sun rises in the morning. Why does it come up just as the Sun goes down?
questions.answer: It is on Earth's far side from the Sun
choices: It is on Earth's far side from the Sun
It sits between Earth and the Sun
It is at its closest point to Earth
It goes all the way round Earth each day
questions.context: At full moon the Moon and the Sun sit on opposite sides of Earth, so as the spinning Earth turns a place away from the Sun at sunset, it turns that place toward the Moon. The Moon takes about 27 days to go round Earth, not one day; its daily rising and setting comes from Earth's spin. Most full moons come when the Moon is not at its closest point.
questions.grade_note: Where the Moon is at full moon, and so why a full moon is up all night, is part of the 6th-grade Sun-Earth-Moon model.

questions.question: Night after night, year after year, people on Earth see the same face of the Moon, with the same pattern of dark patches on it. Why do they never see its far side?
questions.answer: It spins once for each trip round Earth
choices: It spins once for each trip round Earth
It does not spin at all as it goes round
It spins once a day, just as Earth does
Its far side is always in darkness
questions.context: The Moon turns once on its axis in the same time it takes to go once round Earth, about 27 days, so the same side always faces Earth. A Moon that did not spin at all would show every side over one trip round. The far side is not always dark either: it gets as much sunlight as the near side.
questions.grade_note: That the same side of the Moon always faces Earth, because it spins once per orbit, is taught with the 6th-grade Moon's motions.

questions.question: A solar eclipse can happen only at new moon, never at any other phase. Why only at new moon?
questions.answer: Only then is the Moon between the Sun and Earth
choices: Only then is the Moon between the Sun and Earth
Only then is Earth between the Sun and the Moon
Only then is the Moon inside Earth's shadow
Only then is the Moon on Earth's night side
questions.context: In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun's light from part of Earth, and it can do that only from between the two, where it sits at new moon. Then it is in the daytime sky near the Sun, not on Earth's night side. Earth between the Sun and the Moon is the line-up for a lunar eclipse instead.
questions.grade_note: A solar eclipse as the Moon passing between the Sun and Earth, only at new moon, is a named 6th-grade eclipse fact (NGSS MS-ESS1-1).

questions.question: In a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow falls across the Moon and darkens it over a few hours. At which phase of the Moon can that happen?
choices: Only at full moon
Only at new moon
Only at first quarter
At any phase of the month
questions.context: Earth's shadow points straight away from the Sun, and the Moon can move into it only at full moon, when its whole sunlit face is turned toward Earth. At every other phase the Moon is off to one side of the shadow, which is why Earth's shadow cannot be what makes the phases.
questions.grade_note: A lunar eclipse as Earth's shadow on the Moon, only at full moon, is a named 6th-grade eclipse fact, and it is where students meet Earth's shadow on the Moon.

questions.question: During a total lunar eclipse, the whole Moon sits inside Earth's shadow, cut off from direct sunlight. Yet it does not vanish: it glows a dull coppery red. What light makes it glow red?
choices: Sunlight bent through Earth's air
Sunlight bounced off Earth's oceans
Light given off by the Moon's rocks
Sunlight bounced off the other planets
questions.context: Earth's air bends some sunlight round the edge of the planet and into its shadow. On the way, the air scatters away most of the blue light, the same reason sunsets look red, so the light that reaches the Moon is red. The Moon makes no light of its own, the side of Earth facing it is then in night, and the light of the planets is far too faint.
questions.grade_note: The red Moon of a total lunar eclipse is the classic 6th-grade eclipse observation, and it uses the bending of light students met in 5th grade.

questions.question: A new moon comes about once a month, but most new moons bring no solar eclipse anywhere on Earth, not even a partial one. Why does a new moon usually bring no eclipse?
questions.answer: Its tilted orbit usually carries it above or below the Sun
choices: Its tilted orbit usually carries it above or below the Sun
It is usually too far away from Earth to block the Sun
It usually passes behind the Sun instead of in front of it
It is usually on Earth's night side at new moon
questions.context: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to Earth's path round the Sun, so at most new moons the Moon passes just above or below the Sun and its shadow misses Earth. Only when a new moon falls where the two paths cross is there an eclipse, a few times a year. A Moon farther away than usual still makes an eclipse, a ring of Sun round its edge.
questions.grade_note: Why eclipses do not happen every month, the Moon's tilted orbit, is the 6th-grade follow-up to the eclipse line-ups.

questions.question: In a total solar eclipse, the Moon covers the Sun's whole bright face, even though the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon. How can the small Moon hide the huge Sun?
questions.answer: The Sun lies that many times farther away
choices: The Sun lies that many times farther away
The Moon's shadow grows that many times wider on its way to Earth
Earth's air makes the Moon look that many times bigger
The Moon moves out close to the Sun during the eclipse
questions.context: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so the two look about the same size in the sky, the way a coin held close can hide a distant house. The Moon's darkest shadow narrows on its way to Earth, to a strip rarely more than a few hundred kilometres wide, and Earth's air does not magnify the Moon.
questions.grade_note: That the Sun is about 400 times wider and 400 times farther than the Moon is the standard 6th-grade reason a total solar eclipse is possible.
